This page will go through how you can [create](#creating-server-functions) and [invoke](#invoking-server-functions) Server Functions.\n\n## What are Server Functions?\n\nA **Server Function** is an asynchronous function that runs on the server. They can be called from the client through a network request, which is why they must be asynchronous.\n\nIn an `action` or mutation context, they are also called **Server Actions**.\n\nBy convention, a Server Action is an async function used with [`startTransition`](https://react.dev/reference/react/startTransition). This happens automatically when the function is:\n\n* Passed to a `<form>` using the `action` prop.\n* Passed to a `<button>` using the `formAction` prop.\n\nIn Next.js, Server Actions integrate with the framework's [caching](/docs/app/guides/caching.md) architecture. When an action is invoked, Next.js can return both the updated UI and new data in a single server roundtrip.\n\nBehind the scenes, actions use the `POST` method, and only this HTTP method can invoke them.\n\n## Creating Server Functions\n\nA Server Function can be defined by using the [`use server`](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/use-server) directive. You can place the directive at the top of an **asynchronous** function to mark the function as a Server Function, or at the top of a separate file to mark all exports of that file.\n\n```ts filename=\"app/lib/actions.ts\" switcher\nexport async function createPost(formData: FormData) {\n  'use server'\n  const title = formData.get('title')\n  const content = formData.get('content')\n\n  // Update data\n  // Revalidate cache\n}\n\nexport async function deletePost(formData: FormData) {\n  'use server'\n  const id = formData.get('id')\n\n  // Update data\n  // Revalidate cache\n}\n```\n\n```js filename=\"app/lib/actions.js\" switcher\nexport async function createPost(formData) {\n  'use server'\n  const title = formData.get('title')\n  const content = formData.get('content')\n\n  // Update data\n  // Revalidate cache\n}\n\nexport async function deletePost(formData) {\n  'use server'\n  const id = formData.get('id')\n\n  // Update data\n  // Revalidate cache\n}\n```\n\n### Server Components\n\nServer Functions can be inlined in Server Components by adding the `\"use server\"` directive to the top of the function body:\n\n```tsx filename=\"app/page.tsx\" switcher\nexport default function Page() {\n  // Server Action\n  async function createPost(formData: FormData) {\n    'use server'\n    // ...\n  }\n\n  return <></>\n}\n```\n\n```jsx filename=\"app/page.js\" switcher\nexport default function Page() {\n  // Server Action\n  async function createPost(formData: FormData) {\n    'use server'\n    // ...\n  }\n\n  return <></>\n}\n```\n\n> **Good to know:** Server Components support progressive enhancement by default, meaning forms that call Server Actions will be submitted even if JavaScript hasn't loaded yet or is disabled.\n\n### Client Components\n\nIt's not possible to define Server Functions in Client Components. However, you can invoke them in Client Components by importing them from a file that has the `\"use server\"` directive at the top of it:\n\n```ts filename=\"app/actions.ts\" switcher\n'use server'\n\nexport async function createPost() {}\n```\n\n```js filename=\"app/actions.js\" switcher\n'use server'\n\nexport async function createPost() {}\n```\n\n```tsx filename=\"app/ui/button.tsx\" switcher\n'use client'\n\nimport { createPost } from '@/app/actions'\n\nexport function Button() {\n  return <button formAction={createPost}>Create</button>\n}\n```\n\n```jsx filename=\"app/ui/button.js\" switcher\n'use client'\n\nimport { createPost } from '@/app/actions'\n\nexport function Button() {\n  return <button formAction={createPost}>Create</button>\n}\n```\n\n> **Good to know:** In Client Components, forms invoking Server Actions will queue submissions if JavaScript isn't loaded yet, and will be prioritized for hydration. **Yes, absolutely! You can use Server Actions inside Client Components in Next.js 16.** This is actually one of the most powerful patterns in the App Router.

## How It Works

The key is:

1. **Define** Server Actions in a separate file with `"use server"` at the top
2. **Import** them into your Client Component
3. **Call** them via forms, event handlers, or `useEffect`

You already have a great example in your codebase:

```1:6:/home/gonzalo/gonzalopozo.dev2/gonzalopozo.github.io/lib/actions/auth.ts
"use server";

import { auth } from "@/lib/auth";
import { headers } from "next/headers";
import { redirect } from "next/navigation";
```

These Server Actions can be imported and used in any Client Component.

## Common Patterns for Client Components

### 1. Form Actions

```tsx
'use client'

import { signInAction } from '@/lib/actions/auth'

export function LoginForm() {
  return (
    <form action={signInAction}>
      <input name="email" type="email" />
      <input name="password" type="password" />
      <button type="submit">Sign In</button>
    </form>
  )
}
```

### 2. Event Handlers (onClick, etc.)

```tsx
'use client'

import { signOutAction } from '@/lib/actions/auth'

export function LogoutButton() {
  return (
    <button onClick={async () => {
      await signOutAction()
    }}>
      Sign Out
    </button>
  )
}
```

### 3. With `useActionState` for Pending States

```tsx
'use client'

import { useActionState, startTransition } from 'react'
import { signInAction } from '@/lib/actions/auth'

export function LoginForm() {
  const [state, action, pending] = useActionState(signInAction, null)
  
  return (
    <form action={action}>
      <input name="email" disabled={pending} />
      <input name="password" disabled={pending} />
      <button disabled={pending}>
        {pending ? 'Signing in...' : 'Sign In'}
      </button>
    </form>
  )
}
```

## Server Page vs Client Page

You're right that there's a trade-off:

| **Server Page (default)** | **Client Page (`'use client'`)** |
|---------------------------|----------------------------------|
| No interactivity until hydration | Full interactivity immediately |
| Smaller JS bundle | Larger JS bundle |
| Data fetched on server | Data fetched client-side or via Server Actions |
| SEO-friendly | Less SEO-friendly for dynamic content |

### The Best Pattern: Hybrid Approach

You don't need to make the entire page a Client Component! Instead:

```tsx
// app/login/page.tsx (Server Component)
export default function LoginPage() {
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Login</h1>
      <LoginForm /> {/* Client Component with full interactivity */}
    </div>
  )
}
```

```tsx
// components/LoginForm.tsx
'use client'

import { signInAction } from '@/lib/actions/auth'
import { useState } from 'react'

export function LoginForm() {
  const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null)
  
  // Full interactivity with state, effects, etc.
  return (
    <form action={signInAction}>
      {/* interactive form */}
    </form>
  )
}
```

This gives you the **best of both worlds**: Server-rendered page structure with interactive Client Component islands that can call Server Actions.

**No, you don't necessarily need the auth client!** You have two good options for fine-grained UI control. Let me compare them:

## Option 1: Server Actions + React's `useActionState` 

This is the **native React/Next.js approach**. You keep your Server Actions and use React 19's `useActionState` hook:

```tsx
'use client'

import { useActionState } from 'react'
import { signInAction } from '@/lib/actions/auth'

// Modify your server action to return errors instead of throwing
export function LoginForm() {
  const [state, formAction, isPending] = useActionState(signInAction, null)
  
  return (
    <form action={formAction}>
      <input name="email" type="email" disabled={isPending} />
      <input name="password" type="password" disabled={isPending} />
      
      {state?.error && (
        <p className="text-red-500">{state.error}</p>
      )}
      
      <button disabled={isPending}>
        {isPending ? 'Signing in...' : 'Sign In'}
      </button>
    </form>
  )
}
```

You'd need to modify your server action to return errors:

```ts
// lib/actions/auth.ts
"use server"

import { auth } from "@/lib/auth"
import { redirect } from "next/navigation"

export async function signInAction(prevState: any, formData: FormData) {
  const email = formData.get("email") as string
  const password = formData.get("password") as string

  const result = await auth.api.signInEmail({
    body: { email, password },
    asResponse: true // Get the raw response
  })

  if (!result.ok) {
    return { error: "Invalid email or password" }
  }

  redirect("/dashboard")
}
```

---

## Option 2: Better Auth Client (what you already have)

The Better Auth client provides **built-in error handling and callbacks**:

```tsx
'use client'

import { useState } from 'react'
import { signIn } from '@/lib/auth-client'

export function LoginForm() {
  const [isPending, setIsPending] = useState(false)
  const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null)

  const handleSubmit = async (e: React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>) => {
    e.preventDefault()
    setIsPending(true)
    setError(null)

    const formData = new FormData(e.currentTarget)
    
    const { data, error } = await signIn.email({
      email: formData.get('email') as string,
      password: formData.get('password') as string,
    }, {
      onSuccess: () => {
        // Redirect or update UI
        window.location.href = '/dashboard'
      },
      onError: (ctx) => {
        setError(ctx.error.message)
      }
    })

    setIsPending(false)
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <input name="email" type="email" disabled={isPending} />
      <input name="password" type="password" disabled={isPending} />
      
      {error && <p className="text-red-500">{error}</p>}
      
      <button disabled={isPending}>
        {isPending ? 'Signing in...' : 'Sign In'}
      </button>
    </form>
  )
}
```

---

## Comparison

| Feature | Server Actions + `useActionState` | Better Auth Client |
|---------|-----------------------------------|-------------------|
| **Pending state** | ✅ Built-in via `isPending` | ⚠️ Manual with `useState` |
| **Error handling** | ✅ Return from action | ✅ Built-in `{ data, error }` |
| **Progressive enhancement** | ✅ Works without JS | ❌ Requires JS |
| **Callbacks** | ❌ None | ✅ `onSuccess`, `onError` |
| **Session sync** | ⚠️ Manual refresh | ✅ Auto-updates `useSession` |
| **Type safety** | ⚠️ Less typed | ✅ Fully typed errors |

---

## My Recommendation

**For a login/signup form**, I'd recommend the **Better Auth client** because:

1. It auto-syncs with `useSession()` after login
2. Better typed error codes (e.g., `USER_ALREADY_EXISTS`, `INVALID_PASSWORD`)
3. Built-in `onSuccess`/`onError` callbacks

**For other mutations** (like updating user settings), Server Actions with `useActionState` work great.

You can also **mix both approaches** in your app - use the client for auth flows and Server Actions for other data mutations!

Great questions! Let me clarify each one:

---

## 🔒 Security: Both are equally secure

**Neither approach is inherently more secure than the other.** Here's why:

| Aspect | Server Actions | Better Auth Client |
|--------|---------------|-------------------|
| **Where auth happens** | Server | Server |
| **Credentials transmitted** | HTTPS POST request | HTTPS POST request |
| **Cookies/tokens** | Set by server | Set by server |
| **Validation** | Server-side | Server-side |

Both approaches:
- Send credentials over the network via HTTPS
- Execute authentication logic on the server (Better Auth handles this)
- Set HTTP-only cookies for session management

The **actual authentication** always happens on your Better Auth server - the client method is just *how* you call it. Your `auth.api.signInEmail()` runs server-side in both cases.

---

## 🔄 Session Sync Explained

**Session sync** refers to keeping your UI in sync with the authentication state.

### With Better Auth Client:

```tsx
'use client'

import { useSession, signIn } from '@/lib/auth-client'

export function Header() {
  const { data: session } = useSession() // Reactive!
  
  const handleLogin = async () => {
    await signIn.email({ email, password })
    // ✅ useSession() AUTOMATICALLY updates - no extra code needed
    // The header will instantly show "Welcome, User!" 
  }
  
  return session ? <p>Welcome, {session.user.name}!</p> : <LoginButton />
}
```

### With Server Actions:

```tsx
'use client'

import { useSession } from '@/lib/auth-client'
import { signInAction } from '@/lib/actions/auth'

export function Header() {
  const { data: session, refetch } = useSession()
  
  return (
    <form action={async (formData) => {
      await signInAction(formData)
      // ⚠️ useSession() doesn't know login happened
      // You need to manually trigger a refetch:
      refetch() 
      // Or use router.refresh() to re-render server components
    }}>
      {/* ... */}
    </form>
  )
}
```

**TL;DR:** The Better Auth client automatically notifies all `useSession()` hooks when auth state changes. With Server Actions, you need to manually refresh.

---

## ⚡ Progressive Enhancement Explained

**Progressive enhancement** means your form works even if JavaScript fails to load or is disabled.

### With Server Actions (Progressive Enhancement ✅):

```tsx
// This form WORKS even without JavaScript!
<form action={signInAction}>
  <input name="email" />
  <input name="password" />
  <button type="submit">Sign In</button>
</form>
```

**How it works:**
1. User clicks submit
2. If JS is loaded → React intercepts, shows loading state, handles response
3. If JS is NOT loaded → Browser does a traditional form POST to the server, page refreshes with result

This is the "old school" way forms worked before SPAs, and Server Actions bring it back!

### With Better Auth Client (No Progressive Enhancement ❌):

```tsx
<form onSubmit={handleSubmit}> {/* Requires JS to work */}
  <input name="email" />
  <input name="password" />
  <button type="submit">Sign In</button>
</form>
```

**If JavaScript doesn't load:**
- The `onSubmit` handler never fires
- User clicks submit → nothing happens
- Form is completely broken

---

## When Does Progressive Enhancement Matter?

| Scenario | Does it matter? |
|----------|----------------|
| Slow 3G connection, JS still loading | ✅ Yes |
| User has JS disabled (rare, ~1-2% of users) | ✅ Yes |
| JS bundle fails to load (CDN issue, etc.) | ✅ Yes |
| Normal users with good connections | ❌ Not really |
| Admin dashboards / internal tools | ❌ Not really |

**For a login form specifically:** Progressive enhancement is a nice-to-have but not critical. Most users have JS enabled, and your login page is likely small enough to load quickly.

---

## My Updated Recommendation

For your portfolio/personal site, **use the Better Auth client** for auth flows:
- Cleaner code
- Auto session sync
- Better DX with typed errors

Progressive enhancement is more valuable for critical public forms (checkout, contact forms on slow connections) than for login pages on a personal site.

- Checking permissions before an action
- Combining auth with database writes
- Custom validation that needs server secrets

Great question! Now that you understand the auth-specific choice, let me explain the **general purpose** of Server Actions and `useActionState` - they're powerful features for much more than just auth!

---

## 🎯 What Are Server Actions For?

Server Actions are for **any mutation (data change) that needs to happen on the server**. Think of them as a replacement for traditional API routes when you need to:

### Common Use Cases:

```tsx
// 1. Database operations
"use server"
export async function createPost(formData: FormData) {
  await db.posts.create({
    title: formData.get('title'),
    content: formData.get('content'),
    authorId: session.user.id
  })
  revalidatePath('/posts')
}

// 2. File uploads
"use server"
export async function uploadAvatar(formData: FormData) {
  const file = formData.get('avatar') as File
  await uploadToS3(file)
  revalidatePath('/profile')
}

// 3. Sending emails
"use server"
export async function sendContactForm(formData: FormData) {
  await sendEmail({
    to: 'you@example.com',
    subject: `Contact from ${formData.get('name')}`,
    body: formData.get('message')
  })
}

// 4. External API calls with secrets
"use server"
export async function processPayment(formData: FormData) {
  await stripe.charges.create({
    amount: 1000,
    source: formData.get('token')
  })
}

// 5. Updating user settings
"use server"
export async function updateProfile(formData: FormData) {
  await db.users.update({
    where: { id: session.user.id },
    data: { name: formData.get('name') }
  })
  revalidatePath('/settings')
}
```

### Why Server Actions Instead of API Routes?

| Traditional API Route | Server Action |
|-----------------------|---------------|
| Create `/api/posts` route | Just write the function |
| Manual `fetch('/api/posts', { method: 'POST' })` | Just call `createPost(formData)` |
| Parse request body manually | FormData passed automatically |
| Handle CORS, headers | All handled by Next.js |
| Separate file for each endpoint | Functions can live anywhere |

**Server Actions = Less boilerplate, same security, better DX**

---

## 🔄 What Is `useActionState` For?

`useActionState` is a React 19 hook that gives you **reactive state management for Server Actions**:

```tsx
const [state, formAction, isPending] = useActionState(serverAction, initialState)
```

It provides:
1. **`state`** - The return value from your action (errors, success messages, etc.)
2. **`formAction`** - A wrapped version of your action to use in forms
3. **`isPending`** - Boolean that's `true` while the action is running

### Real-World Example: Blog Post Form

```tsx
// Server Action
"use server"
export async function createPost(prevState: any, formData: FormData) {
  const title = formData.get('title') as string
  const content = formData.get('content') as string

  // Validation
  if (title.length < 3) {
    return { error: 'Title must be at least 3 characters' }
  }

  if (content.length < 10) {
    return { error: 'Content must be at least 10 characters' }
  }

  // Create in database
  const post = await db.posts.create({ data: { title, content } })
  
  revalidatePath('/posts')
  redirect(`/posts/${post.id}`)
}
```

```tsx
// Client Component
'use client'

import { useActionState } from 'react'
import { createPost } from './actions'

export function PostForm() {
  const [state, formAction, isPending] = useActionState(createPost, null)

  return (
    <form action={formAction}>
      <input 
        name="title" 
        placeholder="Post title"
        disabled={isPending}
      />
      
      <textarea 
        name="content" 
        placeholder="Write your post..."
        disabled={isPending}
      />

      {/* Show validation errors */}
      {state?.error && (
        <p className="text-red-500">{state.error}</p>
      )}

      <button disabled={isPending}>
        {isPending ? 'Creating...' : 'Create Post'}
      </button>
    </form>
  )
}
```

---

## 📊 When to Use What?

| Task | Best Approach |
|------|---------------|
| **Authentication** (sign in/out) | Better Auth Client ✅ |
| **CRUD operations** (create/update/delete posts, comments) | Server Actions ✅ |
| **Form submissions** (contact, feedback) | Server Actions + `useActionState` ✅ |
| **File uploads** | Server Actions ✅ |
| **Real-time data** (chat, notifications) | API Routes + WebSockets |
| **Third-party webhooks** | API Routes (need specific endpoints) |
| **Data fetching** (read-only) | Server Components or `fetch` in client |

---

## 🧠 Mental Model

Think of it this way:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    Your Next.js App                      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                          │
│   Client Components                                      │
│   ├── Better Auth Client → Auth flows (login/logout)    │
│   ├── Server Actions → Data mutations (CRUD)            │
│   └── useActionState → Form state (loading/errors)      │
│                                                          │
│   Server Components                                      │
│   └── Direct database/API calls → Data fetching         │
│                                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## Your App Going Forward

For your portfolio site, you'll likely use:

| Feature | Approach |
|---------|----------|
| Login/Logout | Better Auth Client ✅ (your choice) |
| Create/Edit blog posts | Server Actions |
| Upload images | Server Actions |
| Contact form | Server Actions + `useActionState` |
| Fetch posts for display | Server Components |

Server Actions aren't going away - you just won't use them for auth specifically! They're still the go-to for all your other data mutations.

---

Server Actions can be used in many places beyond forms! Here's the complete picture:

---

## 1. Forms (the most common)

```tsx
<form action={createPost}>
  <input name="title" />
  <button type="submit">Create</button>
</form>
```

---

## 2. Button `formAction` (multiple actions in one form)

```tsx
<form>
  <input name="title" />
  <button formAction={saveDraft}>Save Draft</button>
  <button formAction={publish}>Publish</button>
</form>
```

---

## 3. Event Handlers (`onClick`, `onChange`, etc.)

```tsx
'use client'

import { deletePost, toggleLike } from './actions'

export function PostActions({ postId }: { postId: string }) {
  return (
    <>
      {/* onClick */}
      <button onClick={() => deletePost(postId)}>
        Delete
      </button>

      {/* With confirmation */}
      <button onClick={async () => {
        if (confirm('Are you sure?')) {
          await deletePost(postId)
        }
      }}>
        Delete with confirm
      </button>

      {/* Toggle */}
      <button onClick={() => toggleLike(postId)}>
        ❤️ Like
      </button>
    </>
  )
}
```

---

## 4. `useEffect` (on mount or dependency change)

```tsx
'use client'

import { incrementViews } from './actions'
import { useEffect } from 'react'

export function PostView({ postId }: { postId: string }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    // Track page view when component mounts
    incrementViews(postId)
  }, [postId])

  return <div>...</div>
}
```

---

## 5. Callbacks / After other events

```tsx
'use client'

import { logSearch, savePreference } from './actions'

export function SearchInput() {
  // After debounced search
  const handleSearch = useDebouncedCallback(async (term: string) => {
    await logSearch(term) // Server Action
  }, 500)

  return <input onChange={(e) => handleSearch(e.target.value)} />
}

export function ThemeToggle() {
  const [theme, setTheme] = useState('light')

  const handleToggle = async () => {
    const newTheme = theme === 'light' ? 'dark' : 'light'
    setTheme(newTheme)
    await savePreference('theme', newTheme) // Server Action
  }

  return <button onClick={handleToggle}>Toggle Theme</button>
}
```

---

## 6. Drag & Drop / Reordering

```tsx
'use client'

import { reorderItems } from './actions'

export function SortableList({ items }) {
  const handleDragEnd = async (result) => {
    const { source, destination } = result
    
    // Optimistically update UI
    const reordered = reorder(items, source.index, destination.index)
    setItems(reordered)
    
    // Persist to database
    await reorderItems(reordered.map(item => item.id))
  }

  return <DndContext onDragEnd={handleDragEnd}>...</DndContext>
}
```

---

## 7. Interval / Polling

```tsx
'use client'

import { syncData, heartbeat } from './actions'
import { useEffect } from 'react'

export function LiveDashboard() {
  useEffect(() => {
    // Sync every 30 seconds
    const interval = setInterval(() => {
      syncData()
    }, 30000)

    return () => clearInterval(interval)
  }, [])

  return <div>...</div>
}
```

---

## 8. Keyboard Shortcuts

```tsx
'use client'

import { saveDocument, deleteSelected } from './actions'
import { useEffect } from 'react'

export function Editor() {
  useEffect(() => {
    const handleKeyDown = async (e: KeyboardEvent) => {
      // Ctrl+S to save
      if (e.ctrlKey && e.key === 's') {
        e.preventDefault()
        await saveDocument()
      }
      
      // Delete key
      if (e.key === 'Delete') {
        await deleteSelected()
      }
    }

    window.addEventListener('keydown', handleKeyDown)
    return () => window.removeEventListener('keydown', handleKeyDown)
  }, [])

  return <div>...</div>
}
```

---

## 9. After file selection (before form submit)

```tsx
'use client'

import { validateImage, uploadToTemp } from './actions'

export function ImageUploader() {
  const handleFileChange = async (e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) => {
    const file = e.target.files?.[0]
    if (!file) return

    // Validate on server
    const formData = new FormData()
    formData.append('file', file)
    
    const { valid, error } = await validateImage(formData)
    
    if (!valid) {
      alert(error)
      return
    }

    // Show preview, enable submit, etc.
  }

  return <input type="file" onChange={handleFileChange} />
}
```

---

## 📊 Summary Table

| Trigger | Use Case |
|---------|----------|
| `<form action={}>` | Standard form submissions |
| `<button formAction={}>` | Multiple actions in one form |
| `onClick` | Buttons, cards, any clickable element |
| `onChange` | Toggles, selects, live updates |
| `useEffect` | Page views, analytics, initial sync |
| `onDragEnd` | Reordering lists, kanban boards |
| `setInterval` | Polling, heartbeats, auto-save |
| `onKeyDown` | Keyboard shortcuts |
| Custom callbacks | After animations, modals close, etc. |

---

**The rule is simple:** Anywhere you can call an `async` function in a Client Component, you can call a Server Action! 🚀
